idiom_name: Cats Effect IOApp: the runtime calls run and executes the IO value
implementation_notes: With an effect system the inversion is total: IOApp supplies the real main method, and the runtime calls your run function and evaluates the IO value it returns, installing interruption handling and computing the exit code. The classic framework base class is replaced by a program value plus a runtime, which keeps the program pure until the edge and is the right form for resource-safe, cancelable applications. Use the actor or framework-callback forms when the component is driven by messages or requests rather than by a single entry point.
pitfalls: Nothing runs until the runtime evaluates the IO: an effect that was never composed into run is silently dead code.
Cancellation and finalisers only work when resources are acquired through the effect system's bracket/resource combinators; plain try/finally around effects does not survive interruption.

variants.name: Message-driven callbacks (Akka actors)
variants.idiom_name: Akka Actor.receive invoked by the dispatcher per message
variants.implementation_notes: An Akka actor is a callback object: the actor system's dispatcher owns the threads and invokes receive (or createReceive) with one message at a time, so your code never selects when it runs. This replaces the framework base class with a partial function installed in the actor, which is the right shape for stateful, message-driven components that need a mailbox and supervision. Use it when message-passing semantics - ordering, back-pressure, supervision - matter more than a single program entry point.
variants.code_sketch:
class Orders extends Actor {                     // dispatcher owns the thread
  def receive: Receive = {                       // called by Akka per message
    case Place(order) => sender() ! accept(order)
    case Cancel(id)   => release(id)
  }
}
val system = ActorSystem("shop")
system.actorOf(Props[Orders]()) ! Place(order)   // you send; it calls you back
pitfalls: receive is invoked sequentially per actor, so blocking inside it blocks that actor's mailbox and can starve the dispatcher - move blocking work to a separate dispatcher or future.
Mutable actor state is safe only through that single-threaded illusion; publishing this or leaking a mutable field to another thread breaks the guarantee.
